sentence: Someone has to describe the router's setup of AI models [CONTRACTS-013] [CONTRACTS-120].
It says which models exist, how they are grouped, and which auto-routers pick a model for each request [CONTRACTS-013] [CONTRACTS-120].
The router, the setup-file loader and the admin requests that add models all ask this part of the system, a shared rulebook, so they agree [CONTRACTS-001] [CONTRACTS-008] [CONTRACTS-010].
Many auto-router mistakes get a plain message saying how to fix them [CONTRACTS-023] [CONTRACTS-025] [CONTRACTS-036].
The rulebook also counts licensed features against a limit [CONTRACTS-063].
It works out which effort levels each model accepts [CONTRACTS-109].
When it goes wrong, an admin sees a change refused, or the proxy will not start [CONTRACTS-008] [CONTRACTS-006].
Or a model shows no effort levels although its operator listed some [CONTRACTS-156].
The Router, the proxy's config loader and its admin endpoints all call these pure rules, so each answers the same way [CONTRACTS-001] [CONTRACTS-008] [CONTRACTS-010].

The rules classify `auto_router/` names, check required settings, and count licensed features and changed scoring rules against caller-supplied limits [CONTRACTS-015] [CONTRACTS-027] [CONTRACTS-063] [CONTRACTS-083].
They also validate routing groups, capture caller settings for baseline requests, and resolve reasoning effort levels [CONTRACTS-120] [CONTRACTS-090] [CONTRACTS-109].
Most return a violation message instead of raising; the routing-group and strategy checks raise [CONTRACTS-023] [CONTRACTS-117] [CONTRACTS-124].
None keeps state or touches the network [CONTRACTS-136] [CONTRACTS-140].
auto-router: a deployment whose provider model name starts with a fixed prefix; the router sorts it by kind; it is not a provider model
proxy: the server in front of the router that loads the setup file and takes admin requests that add or change models
licensed feature: a complexity-router feature whose number of routers is capped by a limit the caller passes in; the proxy takes it from its license
reasoning effort level: a named effort a request can ask a reasoning model for: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max
model group: the public model name callers ask for, which several deployments can share
deployment: one configured entry the router can send requests to: a provider model name plus its settings and model facts
provider model name: the model a deployment is set to call; an auto-router puts its prefix here, not in its public model name
router kind: which of four strategies an auto-router uses: semantic, complexity, adaptive or quality
violation message: a plain reason a setup is refused, returned instead of an error; no message means the check found nothing wrong
complexity settings block: the one settings block that configures a complexity router, and its optional default model setting
dependency: a model an auto-router must be able to reach, with a role such as tier, default or classifier
tier: one level of models a complexity router can send a request to
classifier: the part of a complexity router that chooses a tier for each request; its kind is one setting, heuristic v1 when unset
scoring rules: the heuristic v1 settings, such as tier boundaries and keyword lists, that the tuning quota watches
fingerprint: a hash of the scoring rules a router's settings write out
recorded baseline: each router's fingerprint as the proxy first stored it
router identity: the key a recorded baseline sits under: the database id, or the name and tags from the config file
tuning quota: the limit on how many routers may differ from their recorded baseline at once
tuned router: a heuristic v1 router whose fingerprint differs from its recorded baseline; it holds one slot of the tuning quota
routing group: a named set of model groups with its own routing strategy, or a priority group callers ask for by name
routing strategy: the rule that picks one deployment for a request, such as simple-shuffle
priority group: a routing group that gives each member a priority, which becomes its deployments' order
catalog-mapped: the model catalog gives the deployment a mode and the operator's own model facts give none
model catalog: the built-in table of model facts and prices, read fresh on every call
reasoning switch: the model fact that says whether the model reasons at all
level flag: a yes-or-no fact for one level: none, minimal, low, xhigh or max
declared level list: an explicit list of accepted levels in the model facts
baseline request: the routed request rebuilt for a baseline deployment, with its settings and then the caller's on top
captured settings: the caller's allowlisted request settings, copied, with a read-only top level
When a provider model name lacks the `auto_router/` prefix and carries no auto-router setting, then the naming check returns no violation: it is a regular model
When a regular provider model name carries auto-router settings, then refused: keep the prefix and change the public model name instead
When two non-priority groups share a model, then parsing raises one error naming every conflict; priority groups are exempt
When a group member is not in the model list, then a warning only, and only when the caller passes model names
When the reasoning switch is exactly false, then no levels, whatever the flags or a declared level list say

An auto-router is a deployment whose provider model name starts with a fixed prefix, and the text after that prefix picks its kind: semantic, complexity, adaptive or quality [CONTRACTS-013] [CONTRACTS-015] [CONTRACTS-016].
Each kind needs its own settings before the router can load it [CONTRACTS-019]-[CONTRACTS-022].
The prefix is the exact text `auto_router/`, matched case-sensitively and untrimmed, so a name starting with a capital A is a regular model [CONTRACTS-013] [CONTRACTS-014].

After the prefix, a rest beginning with `complexity_router`, `adaptive_router` or `quality_router` names that kind, by prefix, so `"auto_router/complexity_router-eu"` is a complexity router [CONTRACTS-015].
Every other name under the prefix is semantic, even an empty rest or a doubled prefix [CONTRACTS-016].
The Router decides a deployment's kind only through `classify_strategy_router_model` [CONTRACTS-001].
The required settings per kind are [CONTRACTS-019]-[CONTRACTS-022]:
semantic: a routing config, inline or as a file path, plus a default model and an embedding model [CONTRACTS-019]
complexity: `complexity_router_config` or `complexity_router_default_model`, either one alone [CONTRACTS-020]
adaptive: its own config [CONTRACTS-021]
quality: its config or a default model [CONTRACTS-022]
Health checks and permission checks ask `strategy_router_dependencies` which models a router must reach [CONTRACTS-012].
It reads raw settings only, so a malformed field yields no dependency rather than an error [CONTRACTS-049] [CONTRACTS-050].
When an admin request adds or changes a model, the proxy runs up to three checks in order [CONTRACTS-008].
It asks whether the complexity settings block would load, whether complexity settings sit in the right place, and whether the name fits the settings [CONTRACTS-029] [CONTRACTS-034] [CONTRACTS-027].
The admin gets a failing check's reason back as a status 400 (bad request) error [CONTRACTS-008].
The content check validates the complexity settings block with the router's own settings model, so the proxy refuses a write exactly when the router would refuse to build it [CONTRACTS-029].
An absent block passes, and an empty one takes every default [CONTRACTS-029].

Only the first error is reported; a tier boundaries value that is not a mapping gives `"complexity_router_config is invalid at tier_boundaries: Input should be a valid dictionary. The router would drop this deployment at load time, so the write is rejected instead."` [CONTRACTS-030] [CONTRACTS-158].
An unknown top-level key with a string name passes whatever its value, while a top-level key that is not a string is refused [CONTRACTS-031].
Some nested blocks refuse unknown keys [CONTRACTS-171].
The placement check runs only when the provider model name is a complexity router or either complexity setting is present [CONTRACTS-034].
It refuses top-level keys that belong inside the block, since the provider would reject them as unknown parameters [CONTRACTS-036].
The naming check comes last [CONTRACTS-008].
It never reads the settings' contents, and its messages say how to fix the write [CONTRACTS-023] [CONTRACTS-028].

Loading its config file, the proxy refuses a misplaced setting (only on a deployment carrying complexity settings) or a licensed feature over its limit, before the router could silently drop the deployment [CONTRACTS-010].
Content comes first: The proxy first checks that the complexity settings block would load, whatever the model is called [CONTRACTS-029].
Placement is scoped: The placement check runs only for a complexity router, or when either complexity setting is present [CONTRACTS-034].
Stray settings: Settings written beside the block would reach the provider as unknown parameters, so the proxy refuses the change [CONTRACTS-036].
Name comes last: The name must fit the settings: no doubled prefix, no empty router name, and every required setting present [CONTRACTS-025] [CONTRACTS-026] [CONTRACTS-027].
One reason back: The admin gets the failing check's message back with status 400 [CONTRACTS-008].
On the proxy, a license-based limit caps how many complexity routers may use each licensed feature, such as custom prompts [CONTRACTS-142] [CONTRACTS-063] [CONTRACTS-055].
A second limit caps how many may run with changed scoring rules [CONTRACTS-083] [CONTRACTS-142].
Over the second limit, the proxy refuses the admin's change, and a proxy holding too many changed routers stops at startup [CONTRACTS-008] [CONTRACTS-006].

The licensed features are the heuristic v2 classifier (alone or in a chain), the Capability classifier, the Fuse v2 classifier, and custom tier definitions or operator-written classifier prompts [CONTRACTS-052] [CONTRACTS-053] [CONTRACTS-054] [CONTRACTS-055].
A router claims a feature only when its provider model name is a complexity router, so a quality router with the same settings claims nothing [CONTRACTS-061].

Over the limit, the check returns a message such as `"At most 1 auto-router(s) with classifier_type 'capability' (Capability) can be registered but this would make 2. Use a different classifier or remove an existing Capability router."`, which names no license [CONTRACTS-063].
The tuning quota covers named complexity routers with valid settings on the heuristic v1 classifier, the default [CONTRACTS-075] [CONTRACTS-078].
A tuned router is one whose fingerprint differs from its recorded baseline, or from the shipped defaults when it has none [CONTRACTS-080].
Only the scoring rules feed the fingerprint, so changing tiers uses no slot, nor does changing the classifier within heuristic v1 [CONTRACTS-068] [CONTRACTS-078] [CONTRACTS-083].

When the proxy boots and finds no stored baselines, it records every such router's fingerprint under `auto_router_tuning_baseline_v3`, keyed by router identity [CONTRACTS-006] [CONTRACTS-067] [CONTRACTS-076].
When an edit would leave a router tuned, `tuning_quota_violation` counts it plus every other tuned router, never itself twice [CONTRACTS-083].
So re-editing keeps a slot, and reverting frees it [CONTRACTS-084].
Over the quota the proxy answers `403` with a license remedy appended; here 403 means the quota is full [CONTRACTS-008].
Take two heuristic v1 complexity routers, A and B, with a limit of 1 [CONTRACTS-082]:
0 min, Proxy: boots, finds no baselines; records both fingerprints
1 min, Router A: scoring rules edited; tuned, holds the slot
2 min, Router B: scoring rules edited; refused, quota full (403)
3 min, Router B: only its tiers changed; accepted, no slot used
4 min, Router A: scoring rules edited again; accepted, keeps its slot
5 min, Router A: reverted to its baseline; untuned, slot freed
6 min, Router B: scoring rules edited; tuned, holds the slot
A routing group gives a set of model groups its own routing strategy [CONTRACTS-121].
A priority group is a name callers ask for, and it gives each member's deployments that member's priority as their order [CONTRACTS-003].
Groups pass a fixed series of checks, and the first failure raises an error for the caller setting up the router or the admin saving settings [CONTRACTS-002] [CONTRACTS-007] [CONTRACTS-124].
For a priority group, `apply_routing_group_priority` returns a changed copy and leaves the stored deployment alone; for any other group it returns the same deployment unchanged [CONTRACTS-118].
`parse_routing_groups` checks, in this order [CONTRACTS-120]-[CONTRACTS-130]:

each group builds as a `RoutingGroup`; a priority group needs non-empty, distinct members, a priority for exactly each member, each a whole number from 1 to 9007199254740991 [CONTRACTS-120] [CONTRACTS-122] [CONTRACTS-123]
every name is non-empty, though a name of only spaces passes [CONTRACTS-124]
no group is named `"default"`, which is reserved for the implicit fallback group [CONTRACTS-125]
names are unique; the error names only the first duplicate in sort order [CONTRACTS-126]
each non-priority group's strategy is one of the accepted strategy names, matched exactly; `"priority"` is never a top-level strategy [CONTRACTS-116] [CONTRACTS-117] [CONTRACTS-127]
no model sits in two non-priority groups; one error lists every conflict, and priority groups are exempt [CONTRACTS-128] [CONTRACTS-129]
last, a member missing from the model list only logs a warning line, and only when the caller passes model names [CONTRACTS-130]
A bad strategy argument surfaces only when the Router builds the group's selector [CONTRACTS-132].
The Router adds one rule: a priority group may not share a name with a model or alias, while a non-priority group only gets a warning [CONTRACTS-002].
Each deployment's reasoning effort levels resolve to one of three answers: unknown, known to accept none, or a list of levels [CONTRACTS-109] [CONTRACTS-110] [CONTRACTS-112].
The first rule that applies decides [CONTRACTS-111] [CONTRACTS-113].
Lists follow a fixed display order: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max [CONTRACTS-100].
Callers see a model group's levels in its model information [CONTRACTS-004].
Off wins: An explicit "no reasoning" fact gives no levels, even when flags or a declared level list say otherwise [CONTRACTS-109].
Nothing said: With no reasoning mark and no level flag, a catalog-mapped model accepts no levels and any other model is unknown; a declared level list is not read [CONTRACTS-110] [CONTRACTS-108].
A list wins whole: A valid declared level list beats the level flags, and an empty list means no levels [CONTRACTS-111].
No flags: A reasoning model with no level flag and no list is unknown, not given default levels [CONTRACTS-112].
Built from flags: Medium and high are always in, minimal and low unless switched off, xhigh and max only when switched on [CONTRACTS-113].
For `resolve_supported_reasoning_efforts`, a deployment is catalog-mapped when the model catalog gives it a mode and the operator wrote none [CONTRACTS-108] [CONTRACTS-110].

For a provider-prefixed entry such as azure/gpt-5-mini, each unset level flag, and an unset declared list, falls back to the unprefixed twin entry, but the reasoning switch does not [CONTRACTS-102] [CONTRACTS-103] [CONTRACTS-166].
When levels are built from flags, none is kept unless switched off, except on the azure provider's gpt-5 family, where it must be switched on [CONTRACTS-114].
On every routing attempt, the router stamps a copy of the caller's own settings on the request, or clears the stamp [CONTRACTS-005].
The copy lets a baseline request be rebuilt later for a baseline deployment [CONTRACTS-094].
The copy leaves out credentials, and the capture gives nothing at all when the settings are too large or not plain data [CONTRACTS-090] [CONTRACTS-092].
The stamp holds the output of `capture_baseline_parameters` [CONTRACTS-005].

It keeps only allowlisted top-level keys, such as tools, temperature and token limits, in allowlist order; model, messages, metadata and stream never go in at the top level [CONTRACTS-086] [CONTRACTS-090].
By default it also adds the caller's extra body last, cut down to allowlisted keys plus messages [CONTRACTS-091].
A request with an API key, messages, a temperature of 0.2 and tools keeps only the tools and temperature [CONTRACTS-090].

The capture fails closed, returning None, when the settings exceed an estimated 4194304 bytes or 32768 charges, nest deeper than 32 levels, or are not plain JSON, such as a tuple [CONTRACTS-088] [CONTRACTS-092] [CONTRACTS-148] [CONTRACTS-163].
A successful capture has a read-only top level holding validated copies, so later changes to the caller's objects do not reach it [CONTRACTS-093].
`baseline_request` first captures the baseline deployment's own settings and returns None if that fails [CONTRACTS-094].
It then layers, later beating earlier: the routed request's other keys, the deployment's settings, the caller's settings, and merged tools [CONTRACTS-095].
With extra bodies included (the default), each side's extra body follows its settings [CONTRACTS-095].
When both sides' tools are lists and one is non-empty, the deployment's tools come first, then the caller's [CONTRACTS-096].
Allowlisted settings in the routed request itself never reach the result [CONTRACTS-097].
So routed max tokens 4, deployment 64 and caller 128 give 128 [CONTRACTS-164].

Complexity tiers written in the object form, with a model name inside, are not listed as dependencies, so health checks and permission checks do not cover those models [CONTRACTS-155] [CONTRACTS-012].

A deployment that lists its effort levels but sets neither the reasoning switch nor a level flag ignores its declared level list: no levels if it is catalog-mapped, else unknown [CONTRACTS-156] [CONTRACTS-110].
One unknown deployment makes a whole model group's effort levels unknown, though the merging rule would keep the other deployments' levels [CONTRACTS-004] [CONTRACTS-115] [CONTRACTS-152].
A routing group error saved through the proxy's settings update comes back as status 400 but typed as an authentication error [CONTRACTS-007].

Writing a scoring setting at exactly its shipped default still counts as a change and uses up the tuning allowance, except escalation keywords left at their shipped default [CONTRACTS-070] [CONTRACTS-071].
A limit of zero refuses even the first router, while no limit at all means unlimited [CONTRACTS-133] [CONTRACTS-142].

Two license counts disagree for settings holding both old-name and new-name open-source classifier blocks with the old classifier type name [CONTRACTS-157]. If such stored settings exist, the database count claims the custom-prompt feature and the in-memory count does not, so license checks depend on the path [CONTRACTS-157].
